H&P – Super Detailed Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
31-year-old woman with chronic atopic dermatitis presents with 4–5 day history of markedly worsened, diffuse pruritic, erythematous, dry skin rash consistent with an eczema flare; treated virtually with prescription for topical Betnovate and oral fexofenadine and advised to continue emollients and follow-up in 2 weeks.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Worsening red, sore, very itchy, dry skin rash.  
• Onset/duration: Began “past few days” (≈4–5 days); progressively worse.  
• Location/distribution: Chest, hands, arms; worst in antecubital fossae.  
• Character: Dry, erythematous patches; cracks present; no weeping/exudate; no scratch marks or lichenification reported.  
• Associated symptoms: Denies fever, joint pain, respiratory symptoms, or systemic illness.  
• Exacerbating factors: Scratching increases discomfort.  
• Relieving factors: None reported; usual emollients not relieving.  
• Previous/failed treatments this episode: Daily Diprobase emollient cream, Dermol shower wash, OTC hydrocortisone cream, prior trial of OTC antihistamine (cetirizine) without benefit.  
• Review of systems (pertinent):  
  – Constitutional: No fever, malaise.  
  – Skin: As above; no weeping lesions.  
  – Respiratory: Asthma controlled; no current wheeze or dyspnea.  
  – Musculoskeletal: No arthralgia.  
  – Others: Not discussed.

Past Medical History:
• Atopic dermatitis (eczema) – chronic, currently flared.  
• Asthma – intermittent; uses short-acting β₂-agonist inhaler PRN; no daily controller reported.

Medications:
• Diprobase cream – topical emollient, dose/route/frequency not documented (used daily).  
• Dermol wash – topical emollient wash, dose/route/frequency not documented (used daily in shower).  
• Hydrocortisone 1% cream (OTC) – thin application PRN; “not helping.”  
• Salbutamol (“blue inhaler”) – inhaled PRN for asthma; frequency not documented.  
• Planned today:  
  – Fexofenadine – oral antihistamine, dose/frequency not documented (to be taken daily for 2 weeks).  
  – Betnovate (betamethasone valerate) 0.1% cream – topical corticosteroid, thin layer BID for 2 weeks.

Allergies:
• No known drug allergies.

Social History:
• Residence: London, UK; secure environment during call.  
• Smoking: Not discussed.  
• Alcohol: Not discussed.  
• Recreational drugs: Not discussed.  
• Occupational/financial/lifestyle factors: Not discussed.

Family History:
• Mother – hypothyroidism, migraine.  
• No other relevant family history noted.

Physical Examination:
(Virtual visual inspection)  
• General: Appears well; no distress.  
• Skin: Diffuse erythematous, dry patches with fissuring on chest, arms, hands; pronounced in antecubital fossae; no visible exudate, weeping, lichenification, or secondary infection.  
• No vitals recorded.

Investigations:
• None performed during virtual visit.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Acute widespread atopic dermatitis flare  
  – Assessment: History of eczema with classical distribution; worsening despite emollients and low-potency steroid; no signs of infection.  
  – Plan:  
    • Start Betnovate 0.1% cream thin layer BID × 14 days, then reassess.  
    • Start oral fexofenadine (dose not documented) daily for itch × 14 days.  
    • Continue regular emollients (Diprobase, Dermol) liberally.  
    • Education on fingertip-unit dosing, avoiding scratching, and trigger minimization.  
    • Advise to monitor for side effects (skin atrophy, allergic reaction).  
    • Follow-up: Contact service sooner if worsening; otherwise virtual review in 2 weeks if no improvement.  
    • Prescription sent electronically to Boots pharmacy.

Issue 2: Intermittent asthma (stable)  
  – Assessment: No current respiratory symptoms; uses salbutamol PRN only.  
  – Plan: Continue PRN inhaler; consider formal asthma review at routine primary care visit (not urgent).

Issue 3: Preventive/health maintenance  
  – None discussed; recommend routine GP care for vaccinations, screening as appropriate (not covered in transcript).

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Atopic dermatitis flare – High likelihood: Chronic disease, typical flexural involvement, pruritus, dry erythematous rash, known triggers; aligns with transcript.  
2. Allergic/irritant contact dermatitis – Moderate likelihood: Acute worsening could reflect new exposure; patient denies routine changes, making this less likely but possible contributor.  
3. Scabies infestation – Low–moderate likelihood: Intense pruritus with flexural involvement could mimic; lack of burrows, nocturnal itch, or household spread decreases likelihood.

Quality checks:
● Missing but expected elements: Detailed vitals; complete systems review; smoking/alcohol history; detailed medication doses and frequencies; formal allergy verification beyond drugs (foods/latex).  
● Conflicts between transcript & DDx: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; occasional incomplete sentences but clinically adequate.
